clinicalPearls: Zoonosis caused by Francisella tularensis, a small facultatively intracellular aerobic gram-negative coccobacillus; humans are infected via arthropod bites (ticks, tabanid/deer flies, mosquitoes), inhalation of infectious aerosols, handling infected animals, or ingestion of contaminated water/food (Harrison 22e p.1335-1336).

Take a deliberate exposure history: wild animal contact (rodents, rabbits, hares), inhalation of dust contaminated with their urine or feces, recent tick/fly/mosquito bites, brush-cutting or grass-trimming, handling wood or hay, and walking or hunting in wildlife habitats; cluster cases sharing the same exposure are a clue (Harrison 22e p.1337).

The most common initial manifestation is an influenza-like illness with high fever (acute onset, myalgia, headache, constitutional symptoms); fever may be persistent or intermittent. Incubation is usually 3-5 days but may range from 1 to 21 days (Harrison 22e p.1337).

Inflamed, swollen, tender regional lymph nodes are typical; the initial infection route determines which lymphoid tissue is engaged (skin or pharyngeal entry gives regional nodes; inhalation gives mediastinal/hilar nodes) (Harrison 22e p.1337).

Ulceroglandular form (most common, ~47% of US cases): skin inoculation by a blood-feeding arthropod or direct contact with an infected animal/contaminated material produces a primary ulcer plus tender regional lymphadenopathy; the primary ulcer is often a small skin break with limited inflammation that requires careful examination to detect (Harrison 22e p.1337-1338).
Glandular form (~18% of US cases): regional lymphadenopathy without a detectable primary skin ulcer (Harrison 22e p.1338).

Oculoglandular form (~2% of US cases): conjunctivitis with pronounced local inflammation plus regional (e.g., preauricular) lymphadenopathy, acquired by touching the eye with contaminated fingers or by contaminated aerosol (Harrison 22e p.1338).

Oropharyngeal form (~2% of US cases): acute pharyngitis with pronounced local inflammation following ingestion of contaminated water or food, with cervical/tonsillar lymphadenopathy (Harrison 22e p.1338).

Respiratory/pneumonic form (~17% of US cases): acquired by inhaling contaminated aerosol; more often bacteremic and more likely to progress to severe disease requiring inpatient care, particularly in patients aged 65 and over and those with comorbidities. Onset of a dry cough may occur more than 7 days after the influenza-like illness; engaged lymphoid tissue is in the mediastinum or lung hila (Harrison 22e p.1338).

Typhoidal form (~14% of US cases): an older term for a typhoid-like syndrome with prolonged high fever, fatigue, headache, and nausea; Harrison recommends avoiding the term because most historic typhoidal cases were in fact respiratory/pneumonic tularemia acquired by inhalation (Harrison 22e p.1338).

Routine blood biochemistry is generally unhelpful; findings are nonspecific and may or may not show elevated liver enzymes or hematuria. In a Swedish type B outpatient series, white-cell counts stayed within normal limits in 70% of patients and CRP was only moderately elevated (Harrison 22e p.1338).

When tularemia is clinically suspected, communicate the suspicion to the microbiology laboratory in advance so that cultures are handled safely, because F. tularensis causes laboratory-acquired infection and culture requires BSL-3 containment; it is also a US HHS Tier 1 Select Agent (Harrison 22e p.1335, 1339).
For ulcer sampling, swab the edge of the wound (remove any scab first) and rub firmly so the specimen is slightly blood-tinged to maximize yield (Harrison 22e p.1339).
harrison.pathophysiology: Natural transmission is usually through the skin or by inhalation of aerosols, but ingestion of contaminated food/water can also infect. An extremely low dose of about 10-50 organisms inoculated through skin microtrauma or inhaled suffices to cause disease, whereas roughly 10^6-10^8 organisms are required by the oral route. Tissue-resident macrophages (alveolar macrophages in lung, Langerhans cells in skin) transport the organism via blood and lymphatics to lymph nodes, spleen, and bone marrow; in skin, neutrophils phagocytose F. tularensis early. After uptake, the bacterium escapes the phagosome into the cytosol, replicates, exits the cell, and disseminates. F. tularensis is a 'stealth pathogen' that manipulates host-cell signaling, delaying the immune response and permitting rapid systemic spread. Characteristic tissue reactions are granuloma formation and necrotic foci surrounded by macrophages, lymphocytes, and giant cells in lymph nodes, lung, spleen, kidney, and liver; pulmonary autopsy findings show necrotizing pneumonia with fibrin, cellular debris, and neutrophils. Effective protective immunity requires both B and T cells, and antigen-specific recall T-cell responses can persist 25-30 years after infection or vaccination (Harrison 22e p.1337, 1339).
additionalDifferentials: Lung cancer (pulmonary nodules or dense consolidation can mimic malignancy, prompting CT/PET and biopsy before tularemia is suspected) (Harrison 22e p.1337, 1339)
Unspecified viral infection / 'a severe virus' (Harrison 22e p.1337)
Common skin and soft tissue infection (Harrison 22e p.1337)
infectionMimics: Common skin and soft tissue infection (Harrison 22e p.1337)
nonInfectiousMimics: Suspected tumor with lymphoid tissue engagement (Harrison 22e p.1337)
additionalInvestigations: Laboratory confirmation by recovery of an F. tularensis isolate, detection of F. tularensis-specific antigens or nucleic acids, or detection of specific antibodies by serology (Harrison 22e p.1338-1339)
Direct detection by PCR/nucleic acid testing of clinical specimens is rapid and reliable; for ulcer specimens it is comparable to culture in sensitivity and specificity (Harrison 22e p.1339)

Appropriate specimens for direct detection or culture: ulcer specimens (sampled from the wound edge), lower respiratory tract specimens (sputum, tracheal washing, bronchoalveolar lavage), lymph node biopsies or aspirates, and blood cultures (Harrison 22e p.1339)

Blood culture: F. tularensis is slow-growing and a 10-day incubation is recommended for optimal sensitivity; MALDI-TOF identification from blood cultures is an increasingly common, sometimes unexpected, finding (Harrison 22e p.1339)

Serology (ELISA or microagglutination) is the mainstay in many laboratories and is especially useful when tularemia is suspected at a later stage; antibodies are generally detectable 10-20 days post-infection (Harrison 22e p.1339)

Chest imaging in respiratory tularemia: single or multifocal consolidation, pleural effusion, and hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy; CT may show rounded subpleural consolidations and necrotic lymph nodes; pathology resolution on imaging can be slow and take months (Harrison 22e p.1339)
redFlags: Respiratory/pneumonic form, which is more often bacteremic and may progress to severe disease requiring inpatient care, particularly in patients aged 65 and over and those with comorbidities (Harrison 22e p.1338)
Multiorgan involvement or hemodynamic instability, indicating need for inpatient care (Harrison 22e p.1337)
Host factors increasing risk of severe infection: geriatric frailty, immunosuppression, severe lung and/or heart impairment, and other significant comorbidities (Harrison 22e p.1337)
Lymph node abscess formation, which occurs in about one-third of patients and is associated with antibiotic treatment delay of more than 2-3 weeks after disease onset (Harrison 22e p.1340)
Severe complications reported: adult respiratory distress syndrome, myocarditis, pericarditis, endocarditis, meningitis, osteomyelitis, hepatitis, and renal failure (Harrison 22e p.1340)
harrison.prognosis: Before antibiotics, US case-fatality rates were typically 5-15% and could reach as high as 60% in respiratory/pneumonic tularemia. Recent US surveillance (2006-2021) showed 27 of 903 patients (3.0%) with available outcome data died; treatment with at least one high-efficacy antimicrobial class was independently associated with greatly increased odds of survival. Type A is generally more lethal than type B, though there is heterogeneity among type A genetic varieties. Overall type B fatality is estimated at less than 1% in Sweden, where severe respiratory type B tularemia carried about 1.5% fatality. Recovery (and resolution of imaging abnormalities) may be slow, and some patients report postinfectious persisting fatigue and disability of uncertain cause (Harrison 22e p.1339-1340).
pitfalls: Clinical recognition is challenging, especially if the patient does not spontaneously report fever; tularemia may not be suspected until after extensive and costly investigations, and even in high-endemic areas patients are often initially mistreated for other conditions. A high index of suspicion is critical (Harrison 22e p.1337).
If care is sought several weeks after symptom onset, the acute fever onset may not be reported spontaneously and must be actively elicited (Harrison 22e p.1337).

The primary ulcer can be a small, minimally inflamed skin break that is easily missed or may be undetectable, in which case the disease is classified as glandular rather than ulceroglandular (Harrison 22e p.1338).

Failure to alert the microbiology laboratory to suspected tularemia risks laboratory-acquired infection, as F. tularensis is highly virulent and requires BSL-3 culture conditions (Harrison 22e p.1335, 1339).

Acute-phase serology can be misleading because F. tularensis antibodies persist (single titers can remain above the diagnostic cutoff for at least 1 year), so reliable acute diagnosis should rely on a significant rise between paired sera taken 2-4 weeks apart (Harrison 22e p.1339).
Culture specimens taken from an established lymph node abscess are typically F. tularensis negative (Harrison 22e p.1340).
Tularemia patients do not require isolation because there is no human-to-human transmission (Harrison 22e p.1340).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not provide a formal severity score. Clinically, management level is decided by physical examination of the anatomic site and extent of inflammation (pneumonitis, lymph node inflammation, skin ulcers/pustules, pharyngitis), the rate of progression, and host risk factors: localized symptoms are generally suitable for outpatient care, whereas multiorgan involvement or hemodynamic instability suggests inpatient care. The recognized clinical forms (ulceroglandular, glandular, oropharyngeal, oculoglandular, respiratory/pneumonic, typhoidal) are classified by F. tularensis infection route rather than by severity (Harrison 22e p.1337-1338).
management: Aminoglycoside antimicrobials (streptomycin or gentamicin) as first-line treatment, particularly for severe or pneumonic disease
Fluoroquinolones or tetracyclines (ciprofloxacin or doxycycline) as oral alternatives for milder disease, accepting a higher relapse rate with bacteriostatic agents
Supportive care with antipyretics, analgesia and rehydration
Drainage of suppurative, fluctuant lymph nodes that fail to resolve with antimicrobial therapy
Alert the laboratory to the suspected diagnosis given aerosol infectivity, with public-health notification and consideration of deliberate release when clusters occur
Post-exposure antimicrobial prophylaxis with a fluoroquinolone or tetracycline after a recognised high-risk exposure
Prevention advice including protective clothing, insect-bite avoidance and care when handling wild animals in endemic areas
